en: Petavatthu: Ubbarivagga 6. Kaṇhapetavatthu [The Story of the Black Ghost] Once upon a time, there was a certain woman who lived in a village near Sāvatthī. She was wealthy, possessed of great riches, and had many dependents. She was devoted to her husband and treated him with great respect and affection. When her husband died, she continued to live in that same house, maintaining her former way of life. However, because she had failed to perform meritorious deeds for the sake of her deceased husband, he did not attain a happy rebirth. Instead, he was reborn as a hungry ghost (peta) in a state of suffering. Driven by his craving for the food and drink she enjoyed, he appeared before her in the guise of a man. He stood at the threshold of her house, looking like a servant, and said to her: "My lady, please give me some food and drink. At first, she did not recognize him and thought, "This must be one of my husband's servants. So she gave him a portion of food and drink. But when he ate it, he vanished instantly. She repeated this several times, giving him more and more food and drink, yet he always disappeared after eating. Finally, she realized, "This is surely my husband, reborn as a hungry ghost. Because I have not performed meritorious deeds for his sake, he has fallen into this miserable state. Overcome with grief, she began to weep and lamented: "Alas, what a terrible fate! My husband, who was so dear to me, Has been reborn as a hungry ghost, suffering from hunger and thirst. Because I failed to offer alms on his behalf, He now wanders in misery, seeking food and drink. May I now perform good deeds for his sake, So that he may find relief from his suffering! Having thus reflected, she resolved to practice generosity and perform acts of merit for the sake of her husband. From that day forth, she regularly gave alms to the Sangha and dedicated the merit to him. Through the power of her virtuous intentions, her husband’s suffering gradually diminished, and he eventually attained a favorable rebirth. Thus ends the story of Kaṇha-peta. It serves as a reminder that those who fail to perform meritorious deeds for the sake of their deceased relatives will remain in states of suffering, while those who do so will find peace and happiness. Therefore, one should always strive to perform acts of merit for the benefit of others.
“Arise, Kaṇha! Why do you lie there?
What is the use of your sleeping?
For he who is your own brother—”
The heart and the right eye—
his vital winds grow strong there, and he,
O long-haired one, utters cries of distress.
Having heard those words of Rohiṇeya,
Keśava rose up in great haste.
Distressed by grief for his brother,
why indeed do you appear like one mad,
wandering alone through this entire city?
"You are a hare, you say 'hare,' but what kind of hare do you desire?
One made of gold, or one made of jewels?"
I shall have one made for you, my dear, out of iron, or silver,
or even out of tin, lead, and coral.
There are other hares as well,
whose domain is the forest and the woods;
I shall bring them to you too.
“What kind of hare do you desire?
[He replied: “I do not desire those hares that dwell upon the earth;”
“I desire the moon together with its deer;
bring that down for me, O Keśava.
“Surely he is sweet to his kinsmen,” [he thought].
You will abandon your life;
you desire what should not be desired,
like one who seeks a hare from the moon.
“If it is so, Kaṇha, that you know this,
as you instruct others;
why then did you not [prevent] your son from dying before?
Even now you still grieve.
That which cannot be obtained by a human being,
nor even by a non-human being;
"My son has been born; let him not die!
Where can that which is unobtainable be found?
Neither spells nor root-remedies [can avail]."
O Kāḷa, it is possible to bring back that for whom you grieve as a peta, either by means of medicinal herbs or by wealth.
Those of great wealth and great possessions,
even Kshatriyas possessing entire kingdoms,
who have abundant riches and grain—
They too are neither ageless nor immortal:
the kṣatriyas, brahmins,
vaiśyas, śūdras, caṇḍālas, and pukkusas.
These and others by birth—
none of them are free from aging and death—
even those who recite the mantras.
The contemplation on the Brahman has six factors;
these and other [qualities] belong to those possessed of true knowledge,
yet even they are not free from old age and death.
Even those seers who exist,
self-restrained and practicing austerities,
their bodies too, in due time, [perish].
The ascetics abandon [them].
Having developed themselves, the Arhats have done what was to be done and are free from taints.
“They cast off this body through the exhaustion of merit and demerit.
“Alas, while I am burning, [they say]...”
Like pouring water upon a fire that has been sprinkled with ghee, by sprinkling it with water,
one should extinguish every affliction.
Truly, the dart has been pulled out from my heart,
that sorrow which was lodged within it for me who was overcome by grief.
I have dispelled the grief for my son.
I am one whose arrow has been pulled out;
I have become cool and attained Nibbāna.
"I do not grieve, nor do I weep,
having heard this from you, brother.
Thus do those possessed of wisdom act."
Those who are compassionate turn one back from sorrow,
just as Ghaṭa did for his elder brother.
For one who has such ministers and attendants,
they follow after his well-spoken words.
"The pot [is like] an elder brother.
This is the sixth *Kaṇhapetavatthu*.
